uncited: Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data structures organize volumetric data with non-uniform resolution to efficiently store and render sparse or high-gradient fields.

This family solves the problem of managing hierarchical grids where refinement levels vary spatially, enabling efficient traversal and rendering without processing uniform high-resolution data everywhere.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Tetrahedral Regularization](834-tetrahedral-regularization.md) and [Bezier Tetrahedra Evaluation](1422-bezier-tetrahedra-evaluation.md) by focusing on the hierarchical organization of the data (typically box-based or tetrahedral forests) rather than the specific geometric interpolation or basis function evaluation techniques used during the rendering pass.
All AMR data structures in this family share the principle of hierarchical decomposition.
The domain is partitioned into a coarse base mesh (or root level), which is recursively subdivided into finer elements (children) based on error metrics or feature density.

**Hierarchical Indexing:** Elements are organized in trees (e.g., octrees, quadtree-like structures for tetrahedra) where parent nodes represent coarser volumes and children represent refined sub-volumes.

**Level-of-Detail (LOD) Management:** The structure maintains explicit relationships between parent and child elements, allowing traversal algorithms to skip empty or low-detail regions (empty space skipping) and focus on high-detail areas.
**Boundary Handling:** A critical challenge is maintaining continuity and correct neighbor relationships across level boundaries.
Structures must define how data is interpolated or sampled when a ray crosses from a coarse element into a refined child or a neighboring block at a different level.

**Scalar Aggregation:** To support efficient culling and shading, parent elements often store aggregated scalar statistics (min/max values) of their children, enabling early-out tests during rendering.
Partition the volume into axis-aligned bricks of the same level of resolution.
The concept of Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) originated in computational fluid dynamics and other scientific computing fields to efficiently resolve multi-scale phenomena.
In visualization, early approaches relied on uniform grids or simple hierarchical box structures.
The integration of AMR with ray tracing and volume rendering has evolved to handle the complexity of hierarchical data traversal.
